old: Its deepest root describes a throat closing — the physical squeeze behind an emotional one.
The Latin ancestor meant being troubled or distressed, and gave English a familiar adjective ending in -ious.
It's kin to angst and anger, all descended from a Latin verb meaning to trouble or distress.
clues: This uneasy emotion comes from a Latin verb meaning 'to distress,' which is linked to an Ancient Greek verb meaning 'to choke.'
It is a lingering, nervous unease about what might go wrong, vaguer and longer-lasting than a passing worry, and unlike fear, not tied to a clear present danger.
Doctors diagnose it alongside depression, as in 'social ___ disorder,' and it is related to anger and angst, all tracing back to that idea of choking distress.
